rows.title: Color
rows.text: Your eyes very likely have two kinds of color-sensing cell, where a human has three. In the Eurasian red squirrel, a relative in the same genus as the gray squirrel and the fox squirrel, one kind senses short, blue wavelengths and the other senses middle to long wavelengths. If you are an eastern gray squirrel, your two kinds peak at about 445 and 545 nanometers, and in the fox squirrel they peak at about 450 and 540.
rows.note: Kept to the squirrel genus Sciurus; no record gives a human peak, so the numbers are not compared with a human's.

rows.title: Speed
rows.text: If you are a gray squirrel, a fox squirrel or a Eurasian red squirrel, nobody has measured how fast a flicker your eyes can follow. Among relatives, a compilation of measurements lists American red squirrels at about 60 flashes a second, the same as a human, and golden-mantled ground squirrels at more than 100. The southern flying squirrel follows flicker only up to about 10 to 15 flashes a second.
rows.note: No cff_hz record exists for Sciurus, so the row stays at i. I removed "active at night" for the flying squirrel because no record states it.

rows.title: Field of view and sharpness
rows.text: If you are an eastern gray squirrel, the one squirrel tested read about 4 cycles a degree on a grating test, about an eighth of the 30 a human reads, and fox squirrels tested at about 2. In the Eurasian red squirrel, a relative in your genus, the cone cells are densest in a horizontal streak, and you very likely have the same. Nobody has measured how wide your field of view is or how much of it your two eyes share.
rows.note: No record gives field of view or binocular overlap for any squirrel, so the row says so. The 4 cycles a degree is from a single eastern gray squirrel.
